title: Repair Work
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 34 of 40
content:
Toph came home the next afternoon.

Not to stay.

To talk.

She walked into the courtyard carrying a small bag over one shoulder and stopped with both feet on the stone.

Aang was in the kitchen.

He heard the gate.

His whole body moved toward it.

Then stopped.

That stop mattered.

Toph entered.

Katara came downstairs.

I closed my office door behind me.

Four people stood in the room as if we were meeting for the first time.

Toph pointed at the table.

“Sit.”

Aang almost smiled.

He did not.

We sat.

Toph remained standing.

“I’m going first.”

Nobody argued.

She planted her hands on the tabletop.

“I am not mad because people needed a meeting place.”

Aang nodded once.

“I’m mad because you decided my home could absorb that need without asking me.”

“Yes.”

Toph’s face hardened.

“No explanations yet.”

Aang closed his mouth.

“I spent my whole childhood having people decide what was best around me. Where I could go. What I could learn. Who I could meet. Everybody had a reason. Everybody loved me.”

Her voice cracked on the last sentence.

Katara’s hand moved.

Stopped.

Toph continued.

“So when you volunteered the courtyard, it wasn’t just a courtyard.”

Aang’s eyes filled.

“I know that now.”

Toph slapped the table once.

“Stop saying know.”

Aang inhaled.

“You’re right.”

Better.

Toph folded her arms.

“Your turn.”

Aang sat very straight.

“I’m sorry I offered our home without asking.”

No but.

No because.

No immediate explanation.

“I broke an agreement we made specifically so this house would not become public property because of me.”

Toph’s shoulders loosened a fraction.

“I put you in a position where saying no afterward made you responsible for taking something away from people I had already promised it to.”

Katara looked at him sharply.

That was the part Aang had not understood at first.

He did now.

“I’m sorry.”

Toph waited.

Aang did not ask if she forgave him.

Good.

“I already told the delegation I had no authority to offer the space,” he added. “I did not mention any of you.”

Toph’s chin lifted.

“And?”

“I found them a temporary hall at the school. It’s not ideal, but it’s public and accessible.”

She nodded.

Still no forgiveness.

Katara went next.

“I’m sorry I followed you when you left.”

Toph turned.

Katara’s eyes were steady.

“I stopped at the gate when you told me to. But I shouldn’t have made you say it twice.”

Toph’s mouth tightened.

“I know you were scared.”

“That doesn’t make it okay.”

Toph sat finally.

“Thank you.”

Then she looked at me.

I had hoped to escape.

Of course I had.

“I’m sorry I stayed because I thought Aang needed me more than you did.”

Toph tilted her head.

“You did stay.”

“I know.”

Her eyebrow rose.

I groaned. “You’re right. Bad phrase.”

A tiny smile.

I continued. “I made myself the reasonable one because it felt safer than admitting I was as angry as you.”

Katara looked at me.

Aang did too.

“That wasn’t fair to anyone.”

Toph tapped two fingers against the table.

“No.”

We sat in the discomfort.

Repair was terrible entertainment.

Nobody delivered a beautiful speech that made the wound disappear.

We moved into practical questions.

How did Aang prevent this from happening again?

Not “try harder.”

Systems.

He wrote a standard answer for requests involving household space: I need to ask the other residents. I cannot promise privately shared resources alone.

We added a second rule: no one could volunteer another household member’s time, labor, belongings, or private space without explicit agreement.

Toph demanded this include Appa.

Aang objected that Appa was not a household member in the legal sense.

Toph stared at him.

Aang amended the rule.

Katara proposed a public office for Aang outside the house so visitors stopped arriving at our gate with crises.

I had proposed this months earlier.

Nobody remembered.

I chose not to be unbearable about it.

Mostly.

“Weird,” I said. “Almost as if separating public and private functions might help.”

Toph laughed.

Aang covered his face.

Katara kicked me under the table.

The laughter helped.

It did not erase the argument.

That mattered too.

Finally Aang looked at Toph.

“Are you coming home tonight?”

Toph went still.

He added quickly, “You don’t have to answer now.”

“I know.”

Her fingers traced the table grain.

“I want to.”

Aang exhaled.

Toph heard the relief and immediately pointed at him.

“That does not mean everything is fine.”

“I know—”

He stopped himself.

Toph’s mouth twitched.

“I understand.”

“Better.”

That evening we repaired the courtyard wall.

Not metaphorically.

The storm had cracked it and we had ignored the damage because more urgent buildings needed workers.

Toph could have fixed it in seconds.

She refused.

“You people need character.”

So Aang mixed mortar by hand badly.

Katara corrected the water ratio.

I scraped old mortar from stones.

Toph sat on a stool drinking tea and providing criticism.

“This is abuse,” Aang said.

“This is teaching.”

“You’re not doing anything.”

“I’m supervising.”

Katara pointed her trowel at Toph. “At least hold the wall straight.”

Toph sighed dramatically and placed one palm against the stone.

The wall aligned.

“Happy?”

“Yes.”

“Gross.”

We worked until sunset.

The repaired section did not match the old wall perfectly.

New mortar was brighter. One stone sat slightly out of line because Aang insisted it was “structurally expressive.” Toph said that was what incompetent masons called mistakes.

I liked it.

I could see where the break had been.

I could see where hands had put it back together.

That night, Toph slept in our bed.

No ceremony.

No declaration that the fight had made us stronger.

Sometimes people say that because they need pain to justify itself.

The fight had hurt us.

Repair made us more practiced at repair.

That was enough.

In the dark, Aang whispered, “Toph?”

“What?”

“Thank you for coming back.”

Silence.

Then Toph’s foot kicked his ankle lightly under the blankets.

“Don’t make it weird.”

Katara laughed into her pillow.

I reached into the dark until I found three different hands.

None of them held exactly the same way.

All of them stayed.

For tonight.

Chosen again.

Repair looked embarrassingly ordinary.

Aang asked before inviting anyone over.

Katara stopped translating his intentions for him when he got uncomfortable.

Toph came home when she wanted and left when she wanted, and none of us treated either choice as a referendum on the relationship.

I practiced saying what I needed before resentment made the sentence sharp.

Nobody did this perfectly.

One afternoon Aang asked whether three Air Acolytes could use the courtyard for a meeting.

I was tired. My first instinct was yes, because no felt selfish.

I looked at the closed door of my room.

“Not tonight.”

Aang nodded. “Tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow is fine.”

That was it.

No disappointment performed into guilt. No explanation demanded. No score kept.

Later, Toph found me staring at the empty courtyard.

“You look confused.”

“It was easy.”

“What was?”

“Saying no.”

She made a face. “You’re terrible at easy things.”

“Apparently.”

Toph sat beside me.

“People think boundaries are walls,” I said.

“Walls are useful.”

“I knew you’d say that.”

“They keep roofs up.”

“And sometimes people out.”

“Also useful.”

I laughed.

She bumped her shoulder into mine. “Door’s part of a wall too, genius.”

That stayed with me.

Repair did not mean removing every barrier until love could flow unobstructed through the house.

It meant building doors—and trusting the people on the other side to knock.

The hardest repair came a week later when I forgot the lesson and said yes to a dinner I did not want. By the time everyone arrived, I was brittle with resentment.

Katara noticed first.

“Did you actually want this tonight?”

I opened my mouth and discovered no convincing lie.

“No.”

Aang’s face fell.

Toph groaned. “We literally did this already.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you being weird?”

“Because learning something once apparently does not transform my personality.”

Toph considered that. “Annoying but fair.”

We told the guests the truth: the household had overcommitted. They took the food with them and left without catastrophe.

I stood in the suddenly quiet kitchen feeling foolish.

Katara handed me a plate. “Repair is repetition.”

Aang added, “So is airbending.”

Toph said, “So is headbutting a problem until it gives up.”

I looked at her.

“What? Different schools of thought.”

We ate leftovers in peace. The boundary had failed because I had not used it. It still existed when I reached for it again.

The next time Aang asked about guests, I answered without rehearsing. The next time Katara needed quiet, she closed the kitchen door. The next time Toph left overnight, she told us where she was going because she wanted to, not because anyone required permission.

None of this looked dramatic enough to deserve a chapter in anyone else’s history.

It changed ours anyway.

We were getting better at doors.

We practiced again the next day, because repair turned out to be something we did, not something we finished.
